title: The Science of Baking Bread
summary: How flour, water, salt, and yeast turn into a loaf of bread, from kneading and rising to baking in a hot oven.
poll: Baking bread is more science than cooking.

versions.title: Why Bread Gets Big
versions.text:
Smell that? It is fresh bread. Bread is good to eat. It is fun to make, too.

You need just four things. You need flour. You need water. You need salt. You need yeast.

Flour comes from wheat. The wheat is ground to a fine dust. Add water to the flour. Now you have dough.

Next, you knead the dough. You push it. You fold it. You push it some more. This makes the dough strong and stretchy.

Yeast is a tiny live thing. It is too small to see. It eats the sugar in the dough. Then it lets out a gas. The gas makes small bubbles. The bubbles get stuck in the dough. So the dough puffs up. We say it rises.

Then the dough goes in a hot oven. The heat makes the bubbles grow. The bread gets big. The top turns brown and crisp.

In Saudi Arabia, lots of us love tamees. It is a big, round bread. It is baked in a hot clay oven.

versions.title: Why Bread Gets Big
versions.text:
Do you like the smell of fresh bread? Bread is a food we eat each day. It is also a kind of science!

Most bread needs just four things. It needs flour, water, salt, and yeast.

Flour comes from wheat. The wheat seeds are ground into a soft dust. When you mix flour with water, you get a thick dough.

Next, you knead the dough. You push it, fold it, and turn it. You do this again and again. Kneading makes the dough strong and stretchy.

Yeast is a tiny living thing. It is so small that you can not see it. Yeast eats the sugar in the dough. Then it gives off a gas. The gas makes lots of small bubbles. The stretchy dough traps the bubbles. So the dough puffs up. We say that it rises. Yeast likes a warm place, but too much heat will kill it.

At last, the dough goes into a hot oven. The heat makes the gas bubbles grow. The bread gets bigger. The outside turns brown and crisp.

In Saudi Arabia, many of us love tamees. It is a big, round bread that is baked in a hot clay oven.

versions.title: The Science Inside Bread
versions.text:
Have you ever watched bread bake? A flat lump of dough turns into a tall, soft loaf. This change is a kind of science that you can eat!

Most bread is made from just four things. They are flour, water, salt, and yeast.

Flour is made from wheat. The wheat seeds are ground until they become a soft powder. When you mix flour with water, you get a thick, sticky dough.

Next, a baker kneads the dough. She pushes it, folds it, and turns it again and again. Kneading makes the dough strong and stretchy, a bit like a rubber band.

Yeast is a tiny living thing. It is much too small to see. Yeast feeds on the sugar in the dough. As it feeds, it gives off a gas. The gas makes many small bubbles. The stretchy dough traps the bubbles, so the dough puffs up. Bakers say the dough rises. Yeast works best when it is warm, but too much heat will kill it.

Last of all, the dough goes into a hot oven. The heat makes the gas bubbles grow bigger. The bread swells up. The outside dries out and turns brown and crisp.

In Saudi Arabia, many families buy fresh tamees. This big, round bread is baked on the hot wall of a clay oven.

versions.title: The Science Inside Bread
versions.text:
Have you ever watched a loaf of bread bake? A flat lump of dough slowly turns into a tall, soft loaf with a golden top. This amazing change is a kind of science that you can eat!

Most bread is made from only four ingredients. They are flour, water, salt, and yeast. Salt adds flavor, and it also keeps the yeast from working too fast.

Flour is made from wheat. The wheat seeds are ground until they become a soft powder. When a baker mixes flour with water, the two form a thick, sticky dough.

Next, the baker kneads the dough. She pushes it, folds it, and turns it over and over for several minutes. Kneading makes the dough stronger and stretchier, a little like a rubber band.

Yeast is a tiny living thing, much too small to see. It feeds on the sugar in the dough. As it feeds, it gives off a gas. The gas forms thousands of small bubbles. Because the dough is stretchy, it traps the bubbles, and the dough puffs up. Bakers call this rising. Yeast works best in a warm place, but too much heat will kill it.

Finally, the dough goes into a hot oven. The heat makes the gas bubbles grow even bigger, so the bread swells. The outside dries out and turns brown and crisp.

In Saudi Arabia, many families buy fresh tamees. This big, round bread is baked on the hot wall of a clay oven.

versions.title: The Science of Baking Bread
versions.text:
When you watch a loaf of bread bake, a flat lump of dough slowly grows into a tall, soft loaf with a golden crust. This change may look like magic, but it is really science that you can eat.

Most bread needs only four ingredients: flour, water, salt, and yeast. Flour is made by grinding wheat seeds into a fine powder. The powder is mostly starch, but it also holds proteins. Salt adds flavor and keeps the yeast from working too fast.

When a baker mixes flour with water, the proteins join together to form gluten. Gluten is a stretchy web inside the dough. As the baker kneads the dough, pushing and folding it again and again, the gluten grows stronger and more elastic.

Yeast is a tiny living thing, so small that you need a microscope to see it. When it is mixed into the dough, it starts to ferment. This means it feeds on sugars and gives off a gas called carbon dioxide. The gas forms thousands of tiny bubbles. The gluten web traps the bubbles like small balloons, so the dough rises. Yeast works best in a warm place, but too much heat will kill it.

Finally, the dough goes into a hot oven. The heat makes the gas expand, so the loaf swells. The heat also kills the yeast, and the soft dough sets into bread. The outside dries out and forms a brown, crunchy crust.

People have been baking bread for thousands of years. Long ago, bakers in ancient Egypt noticed that dough left sitting would slowly puff up. They did not know about yeast, but it was already working. Not all bread rises, though. Some flatbreads are made with very little yeast, or none at all, so they stay thin.

In Saudi Arabia, many families buy fresh tamees, a large round bread baked on the hot wall of a clay oven.

Most bread needs only four ingredients: flour, water, salt, and yeast. Flour is made by grinding wheat seeds into a fine powder. This powder is mostly starch, but it also contains important proteins. Salt adds flavor, and it also controls how quickly the yeast works.

When a baker mixes flour with water, the proteins link together to form gluten, a stretchy network inside the dough. As the baker kneads the dough, pushing and folding it repeatedly, the gluten becomes stronger and more elastic.

Yeast is a tiny living fungus, so small that you need a microscope to see it. Once it is mixed into the dough, the yeast begins to ferment. It feeds on sugars and releases a gas called carbon dioxide. The gas forms thousands of tiny bubbles, and the gluten network traps them like small balloons. As a result, the dough rises. Yeast works best when it is warm, but too much heat will kill it.

Finally, the dough goes into a hot oven. The heat makes the trapped gas expand, so the loaf swells even more. The heat also kills the yeast, and the soft dough sets into firm bread. Meanwhile, the outside dries out and browns, forming a crunchy crust.

They did not understand the reason, but invisible yeast from the air was already working. Not every bread rises, however. Some flatbreads are made with very little yeast, or none at all, so they remain thin.

In Saudi Arabia, many families buy fresh tamees, a large round bread baked on the hot wall of a clay oven.

versions.title: The Science of Baking Bread
versions.text:
Anyone who observes a loaf of bread baking will notice a flat lump of dough gradually expanding into a tall, tender loaf with a golden crust, and although this transformation appears almost magical, it is actually the result of chemistry and biology operating together.

Most bread requires only four ingredients: flour, water, salt, and yeast. Flour is produced by grinding wheat kernels into a fine powder, which consists mostly of starch but also contains important proteins. Salt enhances the flavor, and it also regulates how rapidly the yeast works, preventing the dough from rising too quickly.

When a baker combines flour with water, two proteins in the flour connect to form gluten, a stretchy network that develops throughout the dough. As the baker kneads, repeatedly pressing and folding the dough, this network becomes stronger and increasingly elastic, which allows it to stretch without tearing.

Yeast is a microscopic fungus, a single-celled microorganism so tiny that billions can fit in a single spoonful. Once it is mixed into the dough, the yeast begins fermentation, consuming sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas along with small amounts of alcohol. The gas creates thousands of tiny bubbles, and the gluten network traps them like miniature balloons, which causes the dough to rise. Yeast is most active at warm temperatures, but excessive heat will destroy it.

Finally, the dough enters a hot oven. The heat causes the trapped gas to expand rapidly, so the loaf swells even further, while water in the dough turns to steam and the alcohol begins to evaporate. The heat also kills the yeast, and the soft dough gradually sets into firm bread. Meanwhile, the outer surface dries and browns as sugars and proteins react, producing a crunchy, flavorful crust.

People have baked bread for thousands of years. Bakers in ancient Egypt noticed that dough left standing would gradually puff up, and although they could not explain the reason, wild yeast drifting in the air was already at work. Scientists later discovered another hidden helper: natural enzymes in the flour break some of the starch into simple sugars, which provides the yeast with a steady supply of food. Not every bread rises, however, because certain flatbreads contain little or no yeast and therefore remain thin and dense.

In Saudi Arabia, many families purchase fresh tamees, a large circular bread baked against the hot interior wall of a clay oven.

versions.text:

Most bread requires only four ingredients: flour, water, salt, and yeast. Flour is produced by grinding wheat kernels into a fine powder, which consists predominantly of starch but also contains significant proteins. Salt enhances the flavor, and it additionally regulates how rapidly the yeast works, preventing the dough from rising excessively quickly.

When a baker combines flour with water, two proteins in the flour connect to form gluten, a stretchy network that develops throughout the dough. As the baker kneads, repeatedly pressing and folding the dough, this network becomes stronger and increasingly elastic, which enables it to stretch considerably without tearing.

Yeast is a microscopic fungus, a single-celled microorganism so minuscule that billions can fit in a single spoonful. Once it is incorporated into the dough, the yeast begins fermentation, consuming sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas along with small quantities of alcohol. The gas generates thousands of tiny bubbles, and because the gluten network traps them like miniature balloons, the dough gradually rises. Yeast is most active at warm temperatures, but excessive heat will destroy it.

Finally, the dough enters a hot oven, where the heat causes the trapped gas to expand rapidly, so the loaf swells even further, while water in the dough converts to steam and the alcohol begins to evaporate. The heat also kills the yeast, and the soft dough gradually sets into firm bread. Meanwhile, the exterior dries and browns as sugars and proteins react chemically, producing a crunchy, flavorful crust.

People have baked bread for thousands of years. Bakers in ancient Egypt noticed that dough left standing would gradually puff up, and although they could not explain the phenomenon, wild yeast drifting in the air was already at work. Scientists subsequently discovered another hidden helper: natural enzymes in the flour break some of the starch into simple sugars, which provides the yeast with a continuous supply of nourishment. Not every bread rises, however, because certain flatbreads contain little or no yeast and therefore remain relatively thin and dense.

In Saudi Arabia, many families purchase fresh tamees, a large circular bread baked against the scorching interior wall of a traditional clay oven.

versions.title: The Science of Baking Bread
versions.text:
Anyone who carefully observes a loaf of bread baking will notice a flat lump of dough gradually expanding into a tall, tender loaf with a golden crust, and although this transformation appears almost magical, it is actually the consequence of chemistry and biology operating in close cooperation.

Most bread requires only four ingredients: flour, water, salt, and yeast. Flour is produced by grinding wheat kernels into a fine powder, which consists predominantly of starch but also contains significant proteins that will later prove essential. Salt enhances the flavor, and it additionally regulates how rapidly the yeast operates, preventing the dough from rising excessively quickly.

When a baker combines flour with water, two proteins in the flour connect to form gluten, a stretchy network that gradually develops throughout the dough. As the baker kneads, repeatedly pressing and folding the dough, this network becomes progressively stronger and increasingly elastic, which enables it to stretch considerably without tearing.

Yeast is a microscopic fungus, a single-celled microorganism so minuscule that billions can fit in a single spoonful. Once it is incorporated into the dough, the yeast initiates fermentation, consuming available sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas along with small quantities of alcohol. The gas generates thousands of tiny bubbles, and because the elastic gluten network traps them like miniature balloons, the dough gradually rises. Yeast is most active at moderately warm temperatures, but excessive heat will ultimately destroy it.

Finally, the dough enters a hot oven, where the intense heat causes the trapped gas to expand rapidly, so the loaf swells even further, while water in the dough converts to steam and the alcohol begins to evaporate. The heat also kills the yeast, and the soft dough gradually solidifies into firm bread. Meanwhile, the exterior dries and browns as sugars and proteins react chemically, producing a crunchy, intensely flavorful crust.

Bakers in ancient Egypt observed that dough left standing would gradually puff up, and although they could not explain the phenomenon, wild yeast drifting invisibly in the air was already at work. Scientists subsequently identified another hidden contributor: natural enzymes in the flour break some of the starch into simple sugars, which provides the yeast with a continuous supply of nourishment. Not every bread rises, however, because certain flatbreads contain little or no yeast and consequently remain relatively thin and dense.

versions.title: The Science of Baking Bread
versions.text:
Anyone who carefully observes a loaf of bread baking will notice a flat, unremarkable lump of dough gradually expanding into a tall, tender loaf with a golden crust, and although this transformation appears almost magical, it is actually the consequence of chemistry and microbiology operating in close cooperation.

Most bread requires only four ingredients: flour, water, salt, and yeast. Flour is manufactured by grinding wheat kernels into a fine powder, which consists predominantly of starch but also contains significant proteins that will subsequently prove essential to the structure of the loaf. Salt enhances the flavor, and it additionally regulates how rapidly the yeast operates, preventing the dough from rising excessively quickly.

When a baker combines flour with water, two proteins in the flour interconnect to form gluten, a stretchy network that gradually develops throughout the dough. As the baker kneads, repeatedly compressing and folding the dough, this network becomes progressively stronger and increasingly elastic, which enables it to stretch considerably without tearing.

Yeast is a microscopic fungus, a single-celled microorganism so minuscule that billions can fit comfortably in a single spoonful. Once it is incorporated into the dough, the yeast initiates fermentation, metabolizing available sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas along with modest quantities of alcohol. The gas generates thousands of microscopic bubbles, and because the elastic gluten network traps them like miniature balloons, the dough gradually and visibly rises. Yeast is most productive at moderately warm temperatures, but excessive heat will ultimately destroy it.

Finally, the dough enters a hot oven, where the intense temperature causes the trapped gas to expand rapidly, so the loaf swells even further, while water within the dough converts to steam and the alcohol begins to evaporate. The heat simultaneously kills the yeast, and the soft dough gradually solidifies into firm bread. Meanwhile, the exterior dehydrates and browns as sugars and proteins react chemically, producing a crunchy, intensely flavorful crust.

People have baked bread for thousands of years. Bakers in ancient Egypt observed that dough left standing would gradually puff up, and although they could not explain the phenomenon, wild yeast drifting invisibly through the air was already at work. Scientists subsequently identified another concealed contributor: natural enzymes within the flour break some of the starch into simple sugars, which provides the yeast with a continuous supply of nourishment. Not every bread rises, however, because certain flatbreads contain little or no yeast and consequently remain comparatively thin and dense.

In Saudi Arabia, many families purchase fresh tamees, an enormous circular bread baked against the scorching interior wall of a traditional clay oven.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to sell bread in a shop
How simple things turn into bread
Why wheat grows in hot places
Why bread is better than rice
questions.why: The article tells how flour, water, salt, and yeast become a loaf of bread.

wrong.A: The article does not talk about selling bread.
wrong.C: Wheat is named, but the article is not about how it grows.
wrong.D: The article does not compare bread and rice.

questions.stem: Where does flour come from?
options: Salt from the sea
Milk from cows
Clay from the ground
Wheat that is ground up
questions.why: The article says flour comes from wheat that is ground into a soft dust.

wrong.A: Salt is another thing in bread, not where flour comes from.
wrong.B: The article does not talk about milk.
wrong.C: Clay is used for some ovens, not for flour.

questions.stem: What does yeast give off that makes bubbles in the dough?
options: A gas
Water
Salt
Flour
questions.why: The article says yeast eats sugar and gives off a gas that makes small bubbles.

wrong.B: Water is mixed with flour to make dough; yeast does not make it here.
wrong.C: Salt is an ingredient, not something yeast gives off.
wrong.D: Flour comes from wheat, not from yeast.

questions.stem: The article says you knead the dough. What does knead mean?
options: To bake it in an oven
To cut it into lots of small bits
To push and fold it again and again
To let it sit in a cold place
questions.why: The article says when you knead, you push the dough, fold it, and push it some more.

wrong.A: Baking comes later, in the oven.
wrong.B: The article never says to cut the dough.
wrong.D: Kneading is done with your hands, not by letting dough sit.

questions.stem: Why does the dough puff up?
options: Gas bubbles get stuck inside it
The salt makes it swell
The baker blows air into it
The flour turns into water
questions.why: Yeast gives off gas, and the bubbles get trapped in the stretchy dough, so it rises.

wrong.B: The article does not say salt makes dough puff up.
wrong.C: No one blows air into the dough.
wrong.D: Flour does not turn into water.

questions.stem: What would MOST likely happen to dough with no yeast in it?
options: It would turn very sweet
It would turn brown before baking
It would not puff up very much
It would get much bigger in the oven
questions.why: Yeast makes the gas bubbles that make dough rise, so without yeast the dough would stay flat.

wrong.A: Yeast eats sugar; taking it out would not make dough sweet.
wrong.B: The article says bread browns in the oven, not before.
wrong.D: The oven makes the gas bubbles grow, but with no yeast there would be no gas.

questions.stem: How does the author explain the steps of making bread?
options: By comparing bread from many lands
By telling a story about one baker
By listing facts about wheat farms
By telling the steps in order, from mixing to baking
questions.why: The article goes in order: mix flour and water, knead, let the yeast work, then bake.

wrong.A: Only one kind of bread from Saudi Arabia is named.
wrong.B: The article does not tell a story about one baker.
wrong.C: Wheat is named only once; the article is not about farms.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell about tamees at the end?
options: To warn us not to eat it
To link bread science to a bread we know in Saudi Arabia
To show that tamees has no flour
To explain how to build an oven
questions.why: Tamees is a bread many people in Saudi Arabia love, so it connects the science to daily life.

wrong.C: The article does not say tamees has no flour.

Steam that is produced inside the hot oven
Carbon dioxide trapped by gluten
questions.why: The article says natural enzymes in flour break starch into sugars, providing the yeast with food.

wrong.A: Salt regulates the yeast; it is not food for it.
wrong.C: Steam forms in the oven, after the yeast has done its work.
wrong.D: Carbon dioxide is what yeast releases, not what it eats.

questions.stem: Besides carbon dioxide, what does yeast release during fermentation?
options: Gluten
Starch from the ground wheat
Small amounts of alcohol
Salt
questions.why: The article says yeast releases carbon dioxide along with small amounts of alcohol.

wrong.A: Gluten forms from flour proteins and water.
wrong.B: Starch is already in the flour.
wrong.D: Salt is an ingredient the baker adds.

questions.stem: The article says the alcohol begins to evaporate in the oven. What happens to it?
options: It turns into a gas and escapes
It becomes part of the crust
It freezes into crystals
It feeds the yeast again
questions.why: To evaporate means to change from a liquid into a gas, which is why little alcohol is left in baked bread.

wrong.B: The crust forms when sugars and proteins react, not from alcohol.
wrong.C: An oven is hot, so nothing freezes there.
wrong.D: The heat kills the yeast, so it cannot feed.

questions.stem: Why does the loaf swell even more once it is inside the hot oven?
options: Salt stops controlling the yeast
The gluten slowly turns back into soft flour
Heat makes the trapped gas expand while water becomes steam
The hardening crust pulls the soft dough upward
questions.why: The article says heat causes the trapped gas to expand rapidly while water in the dough converts to steam.

wrong.A: The article does not say salt stops working in the oven.
wrong.B: Gluten does not turn back into flour.
wrong.D: The crust forms on the outside; it does not lift the loaf.

questions.stem: What can the reader infer about bread made with flour that forms very little gluten?
options: It would hold fewer gas bubbles and rise less
It would turn brown much faster in the oven
It would need no salt at all
It would need to contain much more yeast
questions.why: Gluten traps the bubbles like balloons, so with weak gluten much of the gas would escape.

wrong.B: Browning comes from sugars and proteins reacting; gluten is not linked to speed.
wrong.C: Salt still adds flavor and regulates yeast.
wrong.D: The amount of gluten does not change the amount of yeast.

questions.stem: Why does the author include the detail about bakers in ancient Egypt?
options: To argue that bread from ancient Egypt was better than the bread people bake today
To show that people used yeast long before they understood how it worked
To explain how to build a clay oven
To prove that flatbread came before raised bread
questions.why: The Egyptians saw dough rise but could not explain it, while wild yeast was already at work.

wrong.A: The article does not judge whose bread was better.
wrong.C: Clay ovens are mentioned only with tamees.
wrong.D: The article does not say which kind of bread came first.

questions.stem: How does the role of heat differ before and after the dough enters the oven?
options: Heat helps gluten form before baking, but the oven's heat destroys the gluten afterward
Heat has no effect until the dough is in the oven
Heat makes yeast grow faster at every stage
Moderate warmth helps yeast work, but intense oven heat kills it
questions.why: The article says yeast is most active at moderately warm temperatures, but the oven's heat kills it.

wrong.A: Gluten forms from mixing and kneading, not from heat.
wrong.B: The article says yeast works best when it is warm, before baking.
wrong.C: Too much heat destroys yeast rather than helping it grow.

checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
